Weaving in trust

Data agents in 2026


Sara Altman
J&J Shiny Day · October 15, 2026






https://pos.it/TODO


A year ago, we were really worried about Databot. Some of those concerns are much less relevant now because the models have improved.
Today I want to talk about what has changed and how we weave trust into the systems themselves so these things work for us.
Because it’s Shiny Day, I’ll spend some time on commons, a new open-source package built on shinychat. First, the story of an eval.
The story of an eval

But this doesn’t mean everything is solved

Keep this a brief qualification: improvement isn’t uniform across tasks. Bluffbench2 asks whether models notice subtle data-quality issues in plots.

github.com/posit-dev/bluffbench2


we showed them plots that look like this take a look at this plot. what do you notice?
one thing that flags my attention is these points through the middle of the cloud that fall exactly on a straight line. this is something i might want to dig into further and make sure nothing strange was happening in the underlying data.
we wanted to see if models would be able to pick up on this kind of subtle visual artifact

github.com/posit-dev/bluffbench2


Models have improved, but not every capability has improved equally. Keep this a qualification rather than a second extended warning story.
This is the jaggedness of model capability: strengths in one task don’t tell us everything about performance on another.

LLMs are jagged


Copied from rstudio/llms, website/slides/slides-02.qmd. A task that seems harder to us isn’t necessarily harder for the model. Capabilities don’t follow a smooth, predictable frontier.

We can’t really make statements like “LLMs can’t do X” because it changes.
Some of the things we worried about a year ago are much less relevant now. We need to update our judgments as the evidence changes.

Advice for working with LLMs

Use the best models
Have a human review the work
Be (a little) afraid


6 months ago we might have said, “use the best model available” now it’s more like use the least expensive model that does a sufficient job at your task, and switch depending on the task.
We’ll come back to this advice at the end of the talk.

section: How do we make data agents trustworthy?
text: How do we make data agents trustworthy?

Our flagship agent is Posit Assistant. Posit Assistant is a coding and data science agent. It’s available in RStudio, Positron, and the terminal. When it’s running inside of your IDE, it works inside of your active R and Python session. You can use whatever model from whatever provider you want with it.


assistant.posit.co

section: Build the environment so that it’s easy to be right
text:
Build the environment so that it’s easy to be right

you control the harness around the model, not the model itself build an environment that makes it as likely as possible that your agent will fall into correctness
don’t control the model control the harness

The pit of success

Photo: Falling into the Pit of Success, Coding Horror


A pit of success: design the environment so that falling into it lands you somewhere good. The harness should make the correct path the easy path.

Code as the foundation

LLMs are good at writing code
Reproducible, transparent, auditable


does the agent have to run code? no – it could do things “in its head,” but then you lose reproducibility and transparency.
llms are good at code
we’ve learned from years of code for analysis…
have the agent write code

section: Design the harness with correctness in mind
text:
Design the harness with correctness in mind

Prompting: prioritize correctness, not progress.
Tools that serve correctness: run code, see your session.
Access to your files and environment to have enough context.


Prompting: prioritize correctness over just moving the analysis forward. Posit Assistant … ” openness to uncertainty and subtlety, and a commitment to statistical rigor … Rather than maintaining a feeling of “moving forward,” call out ambiguities and unclear results.”” Tools: the ability to run code and see your session. Context: give it broad access to your files and environment, so it has a good chance at knowing the correct context to solve the problem.
The harness has to work well with the person, giving them the right amount of information at the right times.

section: Performance improves when the environment makes it easy to be right

Performance improves when the environment makes it easy to be right












Posit Assistant is our coding and data science agent. In the IDE it works with your active R or Python session. Here we compare it with a minimal harness on the intuitive condition of bluffbench. This is a different comparison from the earlier model-update results. Harness design can make a difference without changing the underlying model.

Auto mode and human review


The Simpsons GIF, via Caps N Lock


Repeated permission prompts can turn human review into rubber-stamping. The drinking bird is the joke: an approval click isn’t necessarily review.

Auto mode and human review


Anthropic, Auto mode is now the default in Claude Code (August 7, 2026)


Anthropic made auto mode the default for Pro, Max, and Team plans. In their controlled study with 1,053 paid professional testers, human reviewers blocked 13.6% of dangerous commands and auto mode blocked 89%. One permission prompt per session was replaced with dangerous command text; approving it didn’t execute anything dangerous. This was a test environment, not the testers’ own projects, and isn’t a claim that automation is always safer.
The point is to design review around actual human behavior, not assume that putting a person at every approval step automatically makes a system safer. PLACEHOLDER: Posit Assistant auto-mode comparison, if needed; not researched further.

Code visibility




Code should remain available for inspection, but users don’t need every execution block expanded all the time. Visibility is an interaction-design choice, not a substitute for reproducibility.
Databot originally put executed R/Python code and output directly in chat. Over time we added collapsible blocks and show/hide controls. In April 2026, Hide code became independent of result visibility: users could collapse the code input while leaving results visible.
Ordinary chat still shows data-analysis code by default. Optional hiding, collapsed Bash calls, and Canvas summaries are distinct behaviors, not a blanket switch to hiding R/Python code.
This recording shows expanded R code alongside its execution and plot. It illustrates inspectability; it does not demonstrate clicking Hide code.

Commons records which tools produced the answer. Trust is based on that execution path, not on the model’s confidence in its own answer. trust is deterministic
The citation itself is checked against trusted context. A custom answer is not promoted merely because the model says it used a trusted source.

commons does 3 things

Extract trusted calculations from existing artifacts into a data structure
A harness to give the right context at the right time
A feedback loop to push more queries up the trust ladder over time
